review:
I don’t want to spoil you of anything. So, I’m not gonna review the game normally. But I’m not gonna tell you to “just get it already” either. Instead, I’m gonna tell you WHY you should play it, but with ZERO spoilers.


What this game is:
Dream BBQ is season 2 of “ENA”. Season 1 is a series of four YouTube videos which you can watch for free (and should; they’re great!) and season 2 is this video game; “ENA: Dream BBQ”. Like with most things, it’s best to finish season 1 before starting season 2.

Dream BBQ will release in multiple chapters. Chapter 1 is free and out now, but the rest will cost money when they release individually. I’m not sure if the game be a one-time purchase or if you’ll need to buy each chapter individually. This isn’t a half-baked experience, though, and you’ll get to go on a smaller-scale adventure for a couple of hours with a beginning and end, which is part of one overarching narrative.

(Although, like most things ENA, the narrative is pretty strange, vague and confusing, although that’s all part of the fun.)

Why you should play it (after season 1):
ENA season 1 had beautiful, unique, and bizarre visuals, characters with great, varied designs and distinct personalities, and is generally full of absurd and dark humor. All of which are things I love.

Dream BBQ takes that and turns it into a walking simulator with a few simple platforming elements (although one section so far is kind of difficult), which it translates very well into. I personally like season 2’s protagonist more than season 1’s, even if I liked 1 too.

Conclusion:
So yeah, go and watch season 1 if you haven’t already.
Like it? Play Dream BBQ chapter 1 for free!
Like chapter 1? Play it again for the route that you didn’t pick!
Want more chapters? Wait! 🫠

I thought ENA: Dream BBQ was just going to be another weird indie game.

I was wrong.

The world makes absolutely no sense. The characters talk like they're from completely different realities. The environments look like someone put a dream, a fever dream, and an old computer together and somehow made it playable.

And somehow, it works.

At first, I was mostly laughing.

Then I started getting uncomfortable.

Then I started wondering what the hell was actually happening.

And somehow, I was doing all three at once.

What I love most about ENA is that it never feels like it's trying to explain itself to you. It just throws you into its world and expects you to keep up.

One moment you're talking to a completely bizarre character about something that makes absolutely no sense.

The next, you're walking through an environment that feels strangely beautiful despite looking like it shouldn't exist.

And then something happens that makes you stop and think:

"Wait... what?"

The humor is ridiculous, the visuals are unforgettable, and the soundtrack somehow makes the entire thing feel even more like a dream.

I've played games with clearer stories, better graphics, and much more conventional gameplay.

I don't remember most of them.

I'll remember ENA.

I'll remember the strange characters.

I'll remember the bizarre places.

I'll remember constantly wondering whether I was supposed to understand what was happening.

Some games tell you exactly what their world is.

ENA throws you into its world and lets you figure out what it means to you.

It's confusing.

It's funny.

It's beautiful.

It's unsettling.

And I have absolutely no idea what I just experienced.

100% recommended.

I installed ENA: Dream BBQ expecting a quirky surreal indie game. Instead I accidentally injected pure digital schizophrenia directly into my frontal lobe.

This game does not use normal human logic. Every conversation feels like two broken AI chatbots arguing inside a microwave. Every NPC speaks like they know something horrible about you personally.
One second you’re walking through a beautiful dreamscape.
The next second a creature shaped like a tax fraud accusation asks you to collect meat cubes for spiritual reasons.
And somehow it all makes sense. The Steam page says you “explore strange worlds” and “meet sweet and sour characters.”
That is the biggest understatement since “the ocean is somewhat damp.” The worlds in this game look like a PS2 fever dream that escaped containment. The art style feels like someone fed 2004 internet culture, public access television, lost Flash animations, and a cursed geometry textbook directly into a neural network powered by emotional trauma. And ENA herself? ENA is not a protagonist. ENA is a psychological condition. She talks like a customer support bot moments away from a nervous breakdown. Half the time she sounds deeply concerned. The other half she sounds like she’s about to explode into confetti and unpaid taxes. The soundtrack deserves investigation by international authorities. It sounds like haunted elevator music broadcast from a shopping mall floating in deep space. Somehow every song feels nostalgic for a childhood nobody actually had.

The funniest part is that the game is FREE.

Free.

Joel G and the ENA Team created one of the most visually unique games on Steam and then released it onto the internet like an escaped laboratory specimen. The reviews are “Overwhelmingly Positive,” which makes sense because nobody who survives this experience remains mentally capable of leaving a negative review. People online genuinely debate the lore like they’re decoding ancient scripture. Some fans think ENA committed war crimes. Others think the entire game is symbolic. At one point I laughed. At another point I stared at a floating object for ten minutes because I wasn’t sure if it was an NPC, a building, or a philosophical statement.

10/10.

This is not an indie game.

The most [b] Creatively Ambition [/b] game I have ever played .

From the exaggerated artstyle, abstract ideas, unique characters with their own flare everything in this game sets a benchmark for surreal games.

The fact that this game is free feels almost like an act of charity, yet it’s perfectly thematic. [b]ENA: Dream BBQ[/b]doesn’t feel like a mere "game," but a message and a reflection of a reality we all, unfortunately, live in. beneath the bizarre, unique visuals lies a heavy critique of corporate themes and the systematic exploitation of labor.

To put it simply, it is a direct dig at modern job culture and its pervasive toxicity, portrayed cleverly by characters who each speak in a different languages symbolizing how prevalent it is. It follows you as “ENA,” a laborer doing the jobs of multiple people. yet, instead of being thanked or appreciated, you are constantly ridiculed, mistreated, and of course, handed the ultimate "met expectations" remark at the end, an attitude many have faced.

[b]Art Direction & Surrealism:[/b] Another aspect I enjoyed was how creative the art direction was in this game. It was on another level, and it clearly showed how deep and well prepared everything is. by mainly following the theme of surrealism an art that aims to [i]“release the unbridled imagination of the subconscious”[/i] and [i]“resolve the previously contradictory conditions of dream and reality into an absolute reality, a super-reality”[/i] it pulls all parts of this game together in a creative, weird, yet perfectly cohesive way that left me speechless.

review: ENA: Dream BBQ Chapter 1 is unironically my game of the year (2025) pick. I can't wait for the rest of the chapters!

Such an oddball game. It's so extreme and zany in some of its presentation, but yet it's so entrancing in its very surreal and artsy nature. I'm a sucker for stuff that's out there like this game and I think watching the ENA series on YouTube beforehand definitely helped ease me into the vibes, but it's not a necessity for this game. I love the unnecessary amount of attention to detail this game has. There was a point where I interacted with a hole in the ground that had a skeleton in it and the game said "A body could fit in here." and my brain for some reason thought of the non-interactable mannequins around the map. So imagine my surprise when I tried interacting with one immediately after and it told me "Not that kind." like it knew where my brain was going. There's also details like many characters having several additional lines/voice lines that you would normally miss out on if you don't keep on talking to them after some of their main dialogue. One thing I have to give a massive compliment to is the art department. The character designs are so unique, fun, and a lot of the animations are really well done, some almost feeling straight out of an anime with how fluid they're presented at times. Most of my time spent with this game I was either in awe, laughing at what the hell was going on, or I was just straight up dumbfounded, but in the best way. So yeah absolutely play this if you're down for a very outlandish experience!
The fact that something like this even exists in the first place is a serious artistic miracle

Playing ENA Dream BBQ feels like diving headfirst into a fever dream and it’s fantastic. The game oozes surrealism from every pixel, creating a bizarre yet mesmerizing experience that’s hard to put into words. Its worlds are packed with strange imagery and references that feel straight out of the late '90s internet era everything from LSD Dream Emulator to the Zelda CD-i games and obscure webcore aesthetics. The visuals and sound design work together to craft a dreamlike atmosphere that constantly shifts between unsettling and oddly comforting. It certainly has a unique art direction, experimental storytelling, and it captures the spirit of digital nostalgia. However I can see how some found it confusing or directionless more of an “experience” than a traditional game. If you enjoy surreal exploration games, vaporwave style visuals, or the feeling of wandering through a digital dreamscape, ENA Dream BBQ is absolutely worth your time. It’s weird, it’s wild, and it’s unlike anything else out there.

It's a free first-person adventure you might think is complete but is actually just chapter one with other chapters not released as I write this. Totally different art styles and animations for different characters, sometimes the same one. The landscapes are delightfully strange, like naked legs in a sea of red liquid with a huge eye in the sky. It's like a mash-up of different art directions and the designers couldn't agree on what the final look would be. But it was all intentional, part of the appeal and it has that quirky Japanese vibe that I like... even though it's not Japanese. 

A bunch of characters speak in different languages with subtitles and the writing, while not being completely nonsensical, definitely has absurd, surreal vibes. In fact, it feels like a few characters are bipolar or have multiple personalities, the main character Ena being the most obvious example. The characters also usually have more than one line of text so click on them more than once. The gameplay is mostly exploring, talking to people and getting what they want. The best part for me was planting board members' heads in holes to make their body grow (into a board) and reach higher plateaus. However that section also had the most frustrating part that might make people rage quit: a jumping section on platforms while wind constantly blows you to the left. The game takes between 1.5 to 2 hours depending how much you mess around and if you get stuck (like I did in the labyrinth under a building). Color me intrigued for the follow-ups.

There are legs swimming in their natural habitat. My coworker's feet hurt from the smoke. I was told by a wizard to get a life. I compressed a file so much I exploded. I gave birth to the ultimate board member. I spent an hour looking for the bathroom. I have no idea what is going on and I'm enjoying ever second of it. This game keeps you in a state of constant confusion and you just gotta roll with it.

I really like this concept of all the characters speaking different languages but somehow understanding each other perfectly. The main character we play as is also very cool. The concept of the character, her personalities and voices, her animations, her chara-design, her dialogues, I love everything about her.

I mean, how do I even describe this experience?

This game is a bit impenetrable. It's like jumping into a tv show that's 7 seasons in. You have no context, even though there is a lot of context. And any context you uncover is not only layered beneath heaps of mulch, but is also tinged with so much enigma, sarcasm, and irony.

This is like a soup of weirdness. And that's the selling point, this game is meant to be weird and strange. The game oozes artistry. I was delighting over every new character I met. So many weird designs, so many detailed animations, so many unique voice acting lines in so many different languages and deliveries. There is so much to love here in the presentation.

As a game, however, this flounders. It's a basic puzzler meets walking sim. The entertainment is the experience itself, encountering all the strange characters, and with only minor challenges here and there. But outside of some very simple puzzles and some platforming, the actual game here doesn't have too much to offer. It almost feels like a narrative adventure, choices-matter game, à la Life is Strange or Detroit Become Human, but they decided to shift focus toward puzzles and interactivity instead of character interaction and narrative. But the game just doesn't have enough muscle to lift anything outside of its extremely dynamic presentation.

Which is why it's so hard for me to have a strong opinion about this. I love the artstyle and animation; if this was just an online series like Amazing Digital Circus, I would be enthralled. Alternatively, if this were a game with more meat on its bones, I could praise that. But this is all style and no substance. It is too impenetrable to understand without context, and even though I loved everything I experienced, it's really hard to evoke that love for something that is so absolutely confounding and confusing. I'd be excited to see where they take this in the future.

I happened upon this game while watching VODs of a streamer I follow. Minutes after I saw the fluidity of the animation, differing styles of said animation and art on display, and excellent audio mixing and voice acting, I had to turn the video off and pick it up for myself.

I feel that this is a game akin to an interactive artistic showcase in first person than something to complete or win. There does seem to be a broader narrative/goal, and my understanding is that it's based on a web series that I was aware of but have not watched yet. However, my own experience with this game is marveling at the surprises whether they're a shift in tone, location, style, or objective. You're not always "rewarded" for interacting with things per se, but when you do something usually happens. Thing is, I could never guess what it would be each time.

There's something striking about the character of ENA, too. Not really a hero in any traditional sense, but more of a tasktaker who lives (exists?) and works(?) in a surrealist dimension. There's just something delightful about the duality of her personality. Also, there's something very amusing or humorous about her (even if I don't "get" the joke) that drives me forward. And her design is unique in this way that is hand drawn, flat, yet simultaneously and unmistakably dimensional.

It's clear from the jump that this game's core is rooted in unbridled artistry and passion for creating something to express ideas, or feelings, or thoughts, or something else entirely. But in a lot of ways you just kind of get out of it what you get out of it.

I'm very interested to see how development of this progresses toward its full completion. Until then, download and play it. First chapter is free, so there's absolutely no reason not to give it a shot.

Dream BBQ carries the same ecclectic and irreverent attitude as its source matieral with dialogue that's as layered as it is (occasionally) confusing. Guerra and his team showcase their imaginations and take the player on a surrealist rollercoaster with strange characters, some returning from the web series, some new, and even stranger circumstances.

Wearing its influences on its sleeve, the game's level design is very much akin to LSD Dream Simulator and its progeny, but offers "concrete" objectives to guide the player in the form of jobs. Each job has quirky set-up and payoff that is sure to either tickle, confuse, or horrify players throughout the one-to-three-hour experience.

Even though it's only the first episode of the full experience (with the release of subsequent episodes being currently unknown), ENA Dream BBQ is the perfect preview for those wanting a glimpse inside the crazy and imaginative world that Joel Guerra has to offer. The fact that it's free should give players even more incentive to give it a shot.

I very much enjoyed the whole experience, and the only issue I had was improper glyph display for Nintendo Switch controllers (though the fact that it has controller support is a big plus)

[h1]TL/DR: WORTH IT[/h1]
I'll try to be concise and avoid spoilers, enjoy :3

[h2]Intro[/h2]
My experience, as almost everyone else's, began with original series and I fell in love with the concept. The surrealistic mix of 3D and 2D visuals, languages and audio in the setting of 90s games felt refreshing. The idea of turn it into a real game was just a matter of time

[h2]Details[/h2]
Dream BBQ is one of those games, where your curiosity is rewarded. You want to explore those strange holes? Yeah, go ahead. Wanna let this annoying guy suffocate? Why not lol. The list goes on, Joel made sure to fulfill all our intrusive thoughts. I have 40 hours on record and still haven't seen all gimmicks (yeah I like to prolong the pleasure)

[h2]How to play it:[/h2]
[u][b]Don't speedrun[/b][/u] your first playthrough, pay attention to small details and let your inner child do shenanigans. Explore locations, seek for secrets and catch references

[h2]Dry ratings:[/h2]
[b]Gameplay: 5/10[/b]
- mostly 3D exploration, responsive controls, not source-like (almost no inertia), no serious timings

[b]Visuals and style: 10/10[/b]
- mixed 2D/3D, shift to ps1-like graphics, many hand-drawn sprites, contrasting colorscheme

[b]Audio: 10/10[/b]
- impactful sound effects, location-based, doesn't feel repetetive, most of the dialogues are voice-acted, stereo

[b]Story/writing: 6.8/10[/b]
- the protagonist aims to find [i]the boss[/i] but first has to get rid of the annoying smoke. Along the way, you encounter sidequests that lead to different routes, but eventually you reach the goal. The ending gives a hint at future chapters. Characters are unique, with various attitudes toward the player, leading to funny and surreal interactions. Dialogue, unfortunately, can't brag about interactivity or impact; if you're not a great fan of yapping, can always skip the cutscenes

[b]Performance: 9/10[/b]
- runs at 60 fps on my 10-year-old laptop, actually impressive

[h2]Support:[/h2]
If you're already fan of [i]Ena[/i] or enjoyed the time spent in this game, the DLC floods you with backstage content and hella new secrets, recommended for observation and to support devs

[h2]Honorable mention:[/h2]
One extra feature of this game is language. Specific vocabulary, uncommon phrases and overall speech sometimes feels comically exaggerated in some way. Since english isn't my mother tongue, I found it quite helpful; I actually learned handful useful phrases. Even tho most of them sound silly out of context, that makes it even better

[h3]Ps:[/h3]
That was not concise afterall lol. If you're still reading this, thanks, but fr give this game a chance. If I missed sth or made mistakes, you know what to do. That was fun
